title: Module 7 - Decide the Cell's Fate: Apoptosis, the Cell Cycle, and Mitosis
sourcePages: cell death and cell division.pdf, slides 1-30
mission: Work with blank paper and the slides closed unless a step tells you to look. First, draw two columns labeled APOPTOSIS and MITOSIS. In 90 seconds, write everything you already associate with each word. Open slides 2-14 and build an apoptosis flowchart from trigger to removal; close the slides and redraw it from memory. Open slides 16-29 and make a cell-cycle clock plus a four-frame PMAT comic. Finish by answering the recall and MCQs without looking. Reopen the slides only to repair answers you missed, and write each repair as one short cause -> event -> result chain.
primer: Act it out: curl inward to represent apoptotic shrinkage, make finger 'blebs,' split an imaginary nucleus into fragments, and mime a macrophage engulfing the apoptotic bodies. Say the four events aloud in order.
Build the extrinsic chain from cards or scraps: TNF -> TNFR1 -> TRADD/FADD + procaspase-8 -> caspase-8 -> executioner caspases -> apoptosis. Shuffle it, then restore the order.
Build the intrinsic chain beside it: stress -> BAX/BAK pore in mitochondrial outer membrane -> cytochrome c release -> Apaf-1 + procaspase-9 -> caspase-9 -> executioner caspases.
Sort the BCL-2 family aloud: BCL-2/BCL-XL/MCL-1/BCL-w/A1 oppose apoptosis; BAX/BAK/BOK promote it; BID/BIM/NOXA/BAD are BH3-only inducers.
Point to an imaginary plasma membrane: phosphatidylserine normally faces inward, but flips outward during apoptosis. Say, 'Annexin V detects the outward PS eat-me signal.'
Draw the cycle G1 -> S -> G2 -> M, with G0 branching away. Add one verb per phase: grow, copy, prepare, divide; label interphase as about 90% of the cycle.
Make PMAT physical: condense and dismantle the nuclear boundary; line chromosomes at the equator; pull sister chromatids apart; rebuild nuclei and pinch the cell. Name each stage while moving.

recall.q: Without looking, list four visible or structural features of apoptosis.
recall.a: Cell and nuclear shrinkage, loss of adhesion, surface blebbing, chromatin fragmentation, formation of membrane-bound apoptotic bodies, and rapid phagocytic removal are slide-listed features; any four earn full credit.

recall.q: Why does apoptosis usually avoid a strong inflammatory reaction?
recall.a: Cell contents remain enclosed by intact membranes, apoptotic bodies are rapidly phagocytosed, and this limits leakage and secondary necrosis.

recall.q: Reconstruct the extrinsic apoptosis pathway from TNF binding to execution.
recall.a: TNF binds TNFR1; the receptor recruits TRADD, FADD, and procaspase-8; procaspase-8 activates by cleavage; caspase-8 activates downstream executioner caspases.

recall.q: Reconstruct the intrinsic apoptosis pathway from cellular stress to execution.
recall.a: Stress activates pro-apoptotic BCL-2-family members such as BAX/BAK; mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization releases cytochrome c; cytochrome c joins Apaf-1 and procaspase-9; caspase-9 activates executioner caspases.

recall.q: What does Annexin V reveal, and why?
recall.a: It reveals phosphatidylserine exposed on the outer plasma-membrane leaflet because Annexin V binds PS with high affinity; external PS is an apoptotic eat-me signal.

recall.q: State the defining event of G1, S, G2, and G0.
recall.a: G1: growth, protein synthesis, and organelle duplication; S: nuclear DNA replication; G2: final protein and energy preparation for division; G0: temporary or permanent quiescence outside active cycling.

recall.q: For prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase, give the chromosome headline.
recall.a: Prophase: chromosomes condense; metaphase: chromosomes align at the equator and attach to spindle microtubules through kinetochores; anaphase: sister chromatids separate to opposite poles; telophase: chromosome sets reach the poles and new nuclei form.

recall.q: How does active pRb restrain the cell cycle, and what follows loss of both RB1 copies?
recall.a: Hypophosphorylated pRb binds and inactivates E2F, blocking premature G1-to-S progression. Loss of functional pRb removes that control and permits uncontrolled proliferation, including retinoblastoma.

mcqs.q: Which finding most strongly favors apoptosis rather than uncontrolled membrane rupture?
options: Intact membrane-bound bodies rapidly engulfed by phagocytes
Immediate release of all cytoplasmic contents
Persistent tissue inflammation caused by leaked organelles
Random swelling followed by cell lysis
mcqs.explanation: The slides emphasize intact apoptotic bodies, maintained organelle integrity, and rapid phagocytosis.

mcqs.q: In the receptor-mediated pathway, which initiator caspase is activated at the TNFR1-associated complex?
mcqs.explanation: TRADD, FADD, and procaspase-8 assemble at activated TNFR1; caspase-8 then activates executioner caspases.

mcqs.q: Which event directly follows BAX/BAK-mediated mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization?
mcqs.explanation: BAX/BAK pores allow cytochrome c to leave the mitochondrial intermembrane space.

mcqs.q: An Annexin V-positive cell most directly indicates exposure of which molecule?
mcqs.explanation: Annexin V binds phosphatidylserine after it moves from the inner to the outer leaflet during apoptosis.

mcqs.q: At the end of S phase, each replicated chromosome consists of:
options: Two homologous chromosomes joined at their telomeres
Two sister chromatids held together by cohesins
One chromatid attached to two nuclei
mcqs.explanation: DNA replication creates sister chromatids, which remain associated through cohesins before mitotic separation.

mcqs.q: Chromosomes are accurately aligned on the spindle midplane during:
mcqs.explanation: Metaphase is defined by alignment at the cell equator or spindle midplane.

mcqs.q: Which structure provides the chromosome attachment site for spindle microtubules?
mcqs.explanation: Kinetochores are protein assemblies on specialized chromatin that bind spindle microtubules and motors.

mcqs.q: Active, hypophosphorylated pRb prevents premature S-phase entry mainly by binding:
mcqs.explanation: pRb restrains the G1-to-S transition by binding and inactivating E2F transcription factors.

traps: Do not swap the initiators: extrinsic uses caspase-8; intrinsic uses caspase-9.
Do not call BCL-2 pro-apoptotic: BCL-2 opposes apoptosis, whereas BAX and BAK promote mitochondrial permeabilization.
DNA replication occurs in S phase, not during mitosis; mitosis distributes the already replicated chromatids.
Metaphase means alignment; anaphase means separation. If a stem says 'equator,' think metaphase.
checkpoint: Close everything and draw both apoptosis pathways in under 90 seconds. You pass only if the receptors/adaptors or mitochondria components and the correct initiator caspase appear.
From a blank circle, recreate G1-S-G2-M-G0 and PMAT in under two minutes. Then explain what happens to DNA at each transition.
Answer the eight MCQs twice: first normally, then justify why every wrong option is wrong. Continue only after scoring at least 7/8 without guessing.

title: Module 8 - Control Cell Identity: Potency, Differentiation, and Reprogramming
mission: Start by drawing a potency staircase from totipotent to unipotent and place one example from the slides at each step. Then make a two-column comparison of determination versus differentiation. Use slides 11-16 to sketch blastulation -> inner cell mass -> gastrulation -> three germ layers, adding at least three tissue derivatives per layer. Finally, become the experimentalist: for Till-McCulloch, Gurdon, and Yamanaka, state the input, intervention, observation, and conclusion. Close the slides and teach the whole story in five minutes to an imaginary engineering class.
primer: Say the core distinction aloud: fate is what a cell normally becomes; potency is the range of cell types it can become.
Draw a narrowing funnel labeled totipotent -> pluripotent -> multipotent -> oligopotent -> unipotent. As the funnel narrows, say, 'developmental potential decreases as fate becomes restricted.'
Separate two moments: determination is commitment before visible specialization; differentiation is execution of the specialized morphology and physiology.
Explain cell specialization using one mechanism only: different cells express different subsets of genes, so they contain different subsets of proteins.
Draw a stem cell division with two outputs: one arrow loops back to 'self-renewal'; the other moves toward a specialized cell. Add quiescence as a common adult stem-cell state.

Make a germ-layer body map: endoderm -> digestive tract/liver/pancreas; mesoderm -> kidney/cartilage/bone/spleen/circulatory and lymphatic systems; ectoderm -> nail/hair/dermis/brain/spinal cord/retina.

Turn the reprogramming experiments into a proof ladder: differentiated nucleus can support development (Gurdon/Dolly); defined factors can return differentiated cells to pluripotency (Yamanaka); directed culture can then build organized tissue-like structures such as an optic cup.

recall.q: Distinguish cell fate, potency, determination, and differentiation in one sentence each.
recall.a: Fate is what a cell normally becomes; potency is what it can become; determination is commitment to a fate before obvious visible change; differentiation is the later expression of the specialized program and phenotype.

recall.q: Reconstruct the potency hierarchy from broadest to narrowest.
recall.a: Totipotent -> pluripotent -> multipotent -> oligopotent -> unipotent.

recall.q: What molecular principle makes a differentiated cell behave differently from its progenitor?
recall.a: Differential gene expression: the cells express different gene subsets and therefore contain different protein subsets.

recall.q: Name the three central functional properties of a stem cell.
recall.a: Long or unlimited proliferative potential, self-renewal, and the capacity to differentiate into appropriate specialized cells; adult stem cells may also remain quiescent in tissue niches.

recall.q: What developmental rearrangement creates the germ layers, and what are the three mammalian layers?
recall.a: Gastrulation reorganizes the blastula and produces ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

recall.q: Match each germ layer to at least three derivatives from the slides.
recall.a: Endoderm: digestive tract, liver, pancreas. Mesoderm: kidney, cartilage, bone, spleen, circulatory and lymphatic systems. Ectoderm: nail, hair, dermis, brain, spinal cord, retina.

recall.q: What did Gurdon's somatic cell nuclear transfer result demonstrate?
recall.a: A nucleus from a differentiated tadpole intestinal epithelial cell, transferred into an enucleated Xenopus egg, could in some cases support development into a normal tadpole; differentiation had not irreversibly destroyed the genetic information needed for development.

recall.q: Name the four Yamanaka factors shown and two uses of iPSCs.
recall.a: Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc, and Klf4. Uses include patient-specific disease models, drug screening in target cells, avoiding some ESC ethical concerns, gene correction with CRISPR/Cas9, and producing cells or tissues for future transplantation.

mcqs.q: A cell has committed to become muscle but does not yet look different from neighboring cells. It is best described as:
mcqs.explanation: Determination is commitment to a fate before the cell displays the specialized phenotype.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly orders developmental potential from greatest to least?
mcqs.explanation: Development progressively restricts the range of possible cell fates.

mcqs.q: The immediate basis of different behavior in two differentiated cell types is primarily:
options: Different subsets of genes being expressed
mcqs.explanation: The slides attribute differentiation to differential gene expression and thus different protein complements.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a defining stem-cell capability in the slides?
mcqs.explanation: Adult stem cells are described as often quiescent, with low metabolic activity, rather than continuously highly active.

mcqs.q: Which germ-layer match is correct?
mcqs.explanation: The slides place digestive tract, liver, and pancreas under endoderm.

mcqs.q: In Gurdon's experiment, differentiated donor nuclei were placed into:
mcqs.explanation: The nucleus of the recipient egg was removed before receiving the differentiated intestinal-cell nucleus.

mcqs.q: Which set contains only the four factors shown as sufficient for iPSC generation?
mcqs.explanation: The Yamanaka combination in the slides is Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc, and Klf4.

mcqs.q: In the optic-cup culture example, Activin was used to induce expression of:
mcqs.explanation: The slides describe Activin induction of Rx/Rax, with Rx-positive cells appearing GFP-positive.

traps: Fate and potency are not synonyms: fate is the normal destination; potency is the available range.
Determination comes before visible differentiation. A committed cell can still resemble its neighbors.
Self-renewal makes more stem cells; differentiation makes specialized descendants. Do not swap the arrows.
Do not mix the named gene sets: Oct3/4-Sox2-c-Myc-Klf4 are reprogramming factors; Rx/Pax6/Chx10 and related markers belong to the optic-cup example.
checkpoint: On blank paper, reconstruct the potency funnel and define all five levels. Give a slide example where one is provided.
Draw the blastula-to-gastrula sequence and label all three germ layers with three derivatives each. Complete it in under three minutes.
For Till-McCulloch, Gurdon, and Yamanaka, speak a 20-second input -> intervention -> result -> conclusion summary. Then score at least 7/8 on the MCQs.

title: Module 9 - Defend the System: Barriers, Innate Cells, and the Innate-Adaptive Handoff
sourcePages: Host pathogen interaction.pdf, slides 1-30 (first half: immune-system overview and innate immunity)
mission: Treat the body like a defended engineering system. Draw three layers: boundary defenses, rapid internal innate defenses, and slower specific adaptive defenses. Populate each layer from the slides. Next, follow one bacterium from attempted entry to removal: barrier breach -> chemotaxis -> neutrophil arrival -> phagocytosis -> granule-mediated killing -> inflammatory/adaptive signaling. Then follow one virus-infected host cell to NK-cell killing. End by making a comparison table from memory and completing the recall and MCQs without reopening the deck.
primer: Build the top-level contrast from memory: innate is rapid, broad/nonspecific, and lacks memory; adaptive has a lag, is antigen-specific, and develops memory. Say aloud that the two systems interact.

Sort external innate defenses into three bins: mechanical (skin, mucociliary escalator, flushing), chemical (antimicrobial peptides, stomach HCl, lysozyme), and biological (normal flora competing for nutrients and space).

Sketch the immune supply network: bone marrow generates blood cells; blood and lymph transport immune cells; liver makes complement proteins; lymphoid organs and tissue-resident immune cells support responses.

Turn the typical response into a routing diagram: external barriers first; if breached, phagocytes, antimicrobial proteins, inflammation, NK cells, and complement act; adaptive humoral and cell-mediated responses follow.

Act out neutrophil recruitment: point to an infection, trace a chemical gradient with your finger, move toward it for chemotaxis, engulf the microbe, and 'open' granules containing digestive enzymes and antimicrobial proteins.
Contrast the phagocytes: neutrophils are abundant rapid responders normally in blood; monocytes circulate and become tissue macrophages; macrophages phagocytose in tissues and present antigen.

Model NK-cell selection as a missing-signal detector: a normal cell displays expected surface proteins; an infected or cancer cell may lose some; the NK cell releases perforins and proteases to kill the host cell and its intracellular microbes.

recall.q: Why do the slides call the immune system a functional system rather than a single organ system?
recall.a: Defense is distributed across skin, mucous membranes, secretions, blood cells and vessels, bone marrow, liver-derived complement, lymphatics and lymphoid organs, plus resident immune cells in many tissues.

recall.q: Give the three headline differences between innate and adaptive immunity.
recall.a: Innate immunity has essentially no time lag, is not antigen-specific, and has no memory; adaptive immunity has a lag, is antigen-specific, and develops memory.

recall.q: Give two examples each of mechanical, chemical, and biological external defenses.
recall.a: Mechanical: skin, mucociliary escalator, flushing by saliva/tears/urine. Chemical: antimicrobial peptides in sweat, stomach HCl, lysozyme in tears/saliva. Biological: normal flora occupying space and competing with pathogens for nutrients.

recall.q: Name the internal innate defenses in the typical immune-response diagram.
recall.a: Phagocytic cells, antimicrobial proteins, inflammatory response, natural killer cells, and complement.

recall.q: Why are neutrophils called primary response cells in these slides?
recall.a: They are the most abundant WBCs at about 50-60%, are efficient phagocytes, and rapidly rush to infection sites by chemotaxis.

recall.q: Describe neutrophil action as a five-step chain.
recall.a: Detect chemical cues -> move by chemotaxis -> contact and engulf the microbe -> form an intracellular compartment around it -> use granule digestive enzymes and antimicrobial proteins to kill and digest it; neutrophils can also form NETs and promote inflammation/adaptive responses.

recall.q: Relate monocytes to macrophages and distinguish macrophages from neutrophils.
recall.a: Monocytes circulate at about 2-10% of WBCs, enter tissues, and become macrophages. Macrophages are tissue 'big eaters' that phagocytose microbes and present antigen, whereas neutrophils normally circulate in blood and arrive rapidly.

recall.q: How do NK cells identify and kill target cells according to the slides?
recall.a: Infected or cancer cells may lack normal surface proteins. NK cells recognize this altered or missing-self pattern and release granules containing perforins and proteases, killing the host target and its intracellular microbes.

mcqs.q: Which combination correctly describes adaptive immunity in the slide comparison?
mcqs.explanation: Specificity and memory distinguish adaptive immunity, whose initial response develops after a lag.

mcqs.q: Which is a biological rather than mechanical or chemical barrier?
options: Normal flora competing for nutrients and space
mcqs.explanation: Resident normal flora provide colonization resistance through antagonistic competition.

mcqs.q: Which organ is identified as a source of complement proteins?
mcqs.explanation: The immune-system overview specifically notes that the liver makes complement proteins.

mcqs.q: A WBC moves up a chemical gradient toward bacteria. This is:
mcqs.explanation: The slides identify chemotaxis as the mechanism by which neutrophils find microbes.

mcqs.q: Which leukocyte is the most abundant WBC and a major rapid phagocytic responder?
mcqs.explanation: Neutrophils are listed at about 50-60% of WBCs and as primary response phagocytes.

mcqs.q: A circulating cell enters tissue and differentiates into a 'big eater.' The circulating cell is a:
mcqs.explanation: Monocytes migrate into tissues and become macrophages.

mcqs.q: Which function links macrophages most directly to adaptive immunity?
mcqs.explanation: Besides tissue phagocytosis, the slides list antigen presentation as a macrophage function.

mcqs.q: NK-cell cytotoxic granules contain molecules described in the slides as:
mcqs.explanation: NK cells release perforins and proteases to kill infected or cancerous host cells.

traps: Innate does not mean only barriers: phagocytes, complement, inflammation, and NK cells are also innate.
Neutrophils and macrophages both phagocytose, but neutrophils are abundant rapid blood responders; macrophages are tissue cells derived from monocytes and can present antigen.
NK cells are lymphocyte-like but are not B or T lymphocytes; in this deck they belong to innate immunity.
Humoral adaptive response means antibodies; cell-mediated adaptive response means cytotoxic lymphocytes. Do not assign antibodies to neutrophils or NK cells.
checkpoint: Draw the three-layer defense architecture and correctly place at least 12 slide examples in three minutes: barriers, internal innate defenses, and adaptive defenses.

Narrate a bacterial invasion and a virus-infected-cell response without notes. Your bacterial story must include chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and granules; your viral story must include missing surface signals, perforins, and proteases.
Complete the eight MCQs, then cover the answers and convert every option into a true statement. Continue only after scoring at least 7/8.
